questions.title: Esmolol suits acute perioperative tachyarrhythmia
questions.question: 35 years old patient was operated for inguinal hernia. Surgeon decided to operate him under general anesthesia (GA). After recovery from anesthesia, on routine investigations at ICU, tachycardia and extrasystoles were observed by ICU specialist. For this patient at this stage, which drugs are helpful?

options.A: Esmolol is special beta blocker used in this case
options.B: Ipratropium may be helpful to control tachycardia
options.D: Pindolol is useful in such case

explanations.A: Correct. Esmolol is a cardioselective beta blocker with an ultra-short duration of action, rapidly metabolised by plasma esterases. This makes it easily titratable and quickly reversible, ideal for controlling acute postoperative tachycardia and extrasystoles in a monitored ICU setting. Its brief action is specifically why it is the preferred beta blocker for this acute perioperative scenario, over a longer-acting alternative.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ipratropium is a muscarinic antagonist used for bronchodilation, not a treatment for tachycardia or extrasystoles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist used to stimulate bowel/bladder motility; it does not treat cardiac extrasystoles and could itself provoke bradyarrhythmia rather than help.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pindolol is a beta blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and a longer duration than esmolol, making it less suited to acute, easily-titratable perioperative control.

questions.learning_objective: Identify esmolol as the appropriate ultra-short-acting beta blocker for controlling acute postoperative tachycardia and extrasystoles.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Esmolol is special beta blocker used in this case"

questions.title: Propranolol masks hypoglycemia manifestations
questions.question: In a hypertensive patient who is treated with insulin for diabetes mellitus, which of the following drugs is to be used with extra caution as it masks manifestations of hypoglycemia?

explanations.A: Correct. Propranolol, a nonselective beta blocker, masks the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia -- tachycardia, tremor and palpitations -- that would normally alert a patient to falling blood glucose. This masking effect, rather than a direct metabolic action, is why propranolol needs extra caution in an insulin-treated diabetic patient. Without these warning signs, a hypoglycemic episode can go unrecognised for longer, delaying treatment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prazosin, an alpha1 blocker, does not act on the beta-adrenoceptor-mediated adrenergic symptoms of hypoglycemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diazoxide actually raises blood glucose (by inhibiting insulin release), the opposite concern from masking hypoglycemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, does not mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia the way a nonselective beta blocker does.

questions.learning_objective: Identify propranolol as the drug requiring extra caution in insulin-treated diabetics because it masks the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia.

questions.title: Propranolol does not cause hyperglycemia -- the false statement
questions.question: One of the following statements is FALSE regarding Beta-blockers:

options.A: Atenolol has no effect on blood vessels.
options.B: Propranolol is contraindicated in diabetics as it causes hyperglycemia.
options.C: Propranolol causes vasoconstriction of some blood vessels
options.D: Carvedilol causes vasodilation of some blood vessels

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer (this statement is TRUE). Atenolol, a cardioselective beta1 blocker, has minimal direct effect on peripheral blood vessels compared with a nonselective agent.
explanations.B: Correct as the FALSE statement. Propranolol is not contraindicated in diabetics because it 'causes hyperglycemia' -- its actual diabetic concern is masking the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia, not raising blood sugar directly. This is a common misstatement the question is testing recognition of. The real mechanism (symptom masking) is a different, and in some ways more dangerous, problem than hyperglycemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the answer (this statement is TRUE). Unopposed alpha1-mediated vasoconstriction can occur with nonselective beta blockade (such as propranolol's beta2 blockade removing a vasodilatory counterbalance) in some vascular beds.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer (this statement is TRUE). Carvedilol has additional alpha1-blocking activity, causing vasodilation in some vascular beds, unlike a pure beta blocker.

questions.learning_objective: Identify 'propranolol causes hyperglycemia' as the false statement about beta blockers, recognising that its real diabetic concern is masking hypoglycemia's symptoms.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Propranolol is contraindicated in diabetics as it causes hyperglycemia."

questions.title: Acebutolol: beta1 selective, ISA, membrane-stabilizing
questions.question: The beta adrenergic blocker having BETA 1 selectivity, intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and membrane stabilizing property is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atenolol is beta1-selective but lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and membrane-stabilizing property.
explanations.B: Correct. Acebutolol uniquely combines three properties among these options: beta1 selectivity (cardioselectivity), intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (partial agonism), and a membrane-stabilizing (local anaesthetic-like) property. This specific three-property combination is what the question tests, and none of the other listed beta blockers share all three.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carvedilol is a nonselective beta blocker with additional alpha1-blocking activity, not beta1-selective, and lacks ISA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Metoprolol is beta1-selective but lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and membrane-stabilizing property.

questions.learning_objective: Identify acebutolol as the beta blocker combining beta1 selectivity, intrinsic sympathomimetic activity and membrane-stabilizing property.

questions.title: Acebutolol's ISA can worsen exertional angina
questions.question: Which of the following beta-blockers would be most likely to worsen exertional angina pectoris because of its intrinsic sympathomimetic activity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atenolol lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, so this specific angina-worsening mechanism does not apply to it.
explanations.B: Correct. Acebutolol's intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA) means it acts as a partial agonist, providing some low-level beta-receptor stimulation even while blocking the receptor. This blunts the full heart-rate- and workload-lowering effect that beta blockade is meant to provide during exercise. Because that full suppression is exactly what protects against exertional angina, acebutolol's ISA can specifically worsen it, unlike a beta blocker without ISA.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Propranolol lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, so this specific mechanism does not apply to it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nadolol lacks intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, so this specific mechanism does not apply to it.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that acebutolol's intrinsic sympathomimetic activity can worsen exertional angina by blunting the full heart-rate-lowering effect of beta blockade.
